composition: Nominal composition (wt.%): Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C, with Ni deliberately absent ("Ni-free"). Fe is the base element; 15 wt.% Mn acts as an austenite stabiliser and, together with Al and C, participates in the formation of κ-carbide (L1′2, perovskite-type Fe3AlC) and B2 ordered phases; 10 wt.% Al provides the low-density character and, with C, drives the ordering/precipitation of κ-carbides and B2 intermetallics; 0.8 wt.% C is the interstitial species that occupies the octahedral site of the L1′2 κ structure. The alloy was chosen together with its 5 wt.% Ni counterpart to compare the nano-mechanical properties of the ordered NiAl- versus FeAl-type B2 compounds and of the κ-phase that form in both grades. Note: the alloy is designated Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C throughout the abstract, introduction, methods and conclusions, but is printed as Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.5C in Tables 1 and 2 — an apparent typographical inconsistency in the paper.
conclusions: This sample is the as-quenched baseline of the Ni-free Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C lightweight steel: a duplex γ + α structure whose individual phase hardnesses are ≈4 GPa (γ) and ≈3 GPa (α), measured by nano-indentation. It anchors the study's central comparison, that the addition of Ni raises the hardness of B2-bearing structures (peak hardness rising from 7.2 GPa without Ni to 9 GPa with Ni) in both austenite and ferrite, because of the replacement of Fe-Al bonds by stronger Ni-Al bonds. After annealing, the Ni-free grade develops FeAl-type B2 (coarse particles 2–4 μm, plus nano-sized discs ≈200 nm at 900–1050 °C) and needle-like κ-carbides in α (width 200 ± 33 nm at 500 °C, 500 ± 33 nm at 700 °C), giving composite hardnesses of 5.3–6.7 GPa (α + κ) and 8.3–8.9 GPa (α + B2) — consistently below the Ni-containing counterparts (α + B2 up to 13.5 GPa at 1050 °C). The broader significance is both scientific and economic: individual ordered phases and matrix can be resolved mechanically, and low-density steels can reach useful properties with the minimum amount of Ni, which is attractive for light-weighting automotive structures.
mechanisms: In the solution-treated as-quenched state the alloy contains no ordered precipitates, so its hardness reflects the intrinsic resistance of the two single phases; the measured values of ~4 GPa for γ and ~3 GPa for α therefore serve as the baseline against which all annealed (precipitate-bearing) conditions and the Ni-containing grade are compared.

The solution-treated Ni-free phases are slightly softer (γ 4.0 vs 4.2 GPa; α 3.0 vs 3.1 GPa) than their Ni-containing counterparts, an effect rationalised in the study by the stronger Ni-Al bonding compared with Fe-Al bonding, which makes Ni-bearing B2-type structures harder; in the Ni-free alloy the B2 ordering tendency is FeAl-type.

DFT calculations show that substitution of Fe by Mn in the Fe3AlC-κ structure expands the lattice parameter (from 3.78 Å for Fe2MnAlC to 3.84 Å for Mn3AlC) because of the larger atomic radius of Mn (1.61 Å) vs Fe (1.56 Å), and increases all elastic constants; this reflects stronger Mn-C bonds relative to Fe-C bonds and explains why Mn-enriched κ-carbide is harder.

Insertion of C into the octahedral interstitial site of Fe3Al-L12 to form Fe3AlC (κ) rigidifies the structure — giving it the largest tabulated C11 (450 GPa, versus 273 GPa for FeAl and 181 GPa for Fe3Al) — as a direct manifestation of strong Fe-C bonds along the <100> directions; the same phase shows a strong elastic anisotropy (Cα = 2.39), so its E111 is smaller than its E100.

Ordered FeAl-B2 has a low degree of elastic anisotropy (Cα = 0.54), consistent with phase-field simulations of the B2 intermetallic; by contrast, Fe3AlC-κ shows Cα > 1, which is unusual for metals and underpins its un-shearable character (its shear modulus exceeds that of FeAl or Fe3Al).

Per the Orowan mechanism the increase in shear stress is proportional to the inverse of precipitate diameter (Δτ ∝ R−1), so the finely dispersed nano-sized B2 discs that form in α-ferrite on annealing raise the shear resistance of the matrix — the rationale for the high hardness measured for α + B2 composites in these alloys.

κ-carbides are intrinsically less shear-resistant than B2 intermetallics, yet adding brittle nano-sized κ to a γ + micron-sized B2 composite still raises the hardness of the composite, showing that the two ordered phases harden the austenite by different, additive contributions.
microstructure: In the solution-treated (as-quenched) starting state the alloy has a duplex microstructure consisting of the γ (austenite) and α (ferrite) phases; the state is described as containing the γ and α single phases, i.e. without the ordered precipitates (nano-sized cuboid κ in γ, needle-like κ in α, coarse B2 particles and B2 stringers) that develop only upon subsequent annealing. No grain size, phase volume fraction, texture or defect data are reported for this as-quenched condition.
processing: The experimental alloy was melted in an induction furnace. It was then solution heat-treated for 35 min at 1250 °C in a protective argon atmosphere and water quenched. The material was subsequently cut into samples 3 mm (length) × 3 mm (width) × 1 mm (thickness) for nano-indentation. This solution treatment plus water quench defines the as-quenched starting state of the study; the four annealing treatments (500 °C, 700 °C, 900 °C and 1050 °C) that generate the ordered precipitates were applied to this starting material and are not part of this sample's process route.
properties: Nano-indentation hardness of the as-quenched single phases (Ni-free sample): γ ≈ 4 GPa and α ≈ 3 GPa. Test conditions: constant loading/unloading rate of 500 μN s−1 up to a maximum load of 10000 μN with a 20 s hold; each phase measured at least 25 times within arrays of 50–70 indentations on 3 mm × 3 mm × 1 mm specimens. Comparison with the Ni-containing sister alloy in the same solution-treated condition: γ 4.2 GPa and α 3.1 GPa, i.e. the Ni-free sample is slightly softer in the as-quenched state. No tensile, fracture, fatigue, creep or physical/chemical property data are reported for this condition. Characterization techniques available to the study include: transmission electron microscopy (JEOL 2000FX) with selected-area diffraction patterns and bright-field imaging on thin foils prepared by twin-jet electro-polishing in 10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol at 25 V; field emission scanning electron microscopy (Carl Zeiss Sigma) at 20 kV with X-ray EDS on specimens polished and etched in 5% nital; and nano-indentation.
summary: Ni-free duplex lightweight steel Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C (wt.%) in its solution-treated (as-quenched) state, obtained by induction melting followed by 35 min at 1250 °C under protective argon and water quenching. It is the starting condition of the Ni-free grade investigated in a study that combined nano-indentation with ab-initio (DFT) calculations to establish the hardness of individual ordered phases and matrices in Fe-Mn-Al-C low-density steels as a function of annealing temperature (500–1050 °C) and precipitate composition, and to isolate the effect of Ni addition. In the as-quenched state the alloy is a duplex γ (austenite) + α (ferrite) structure without ordered precipitates, with phase hardness of about 4 GPa (γ) and 3 GPa (α).
unmapped: Composition inconsistency in the source: the Ni-free alloy is written Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C in the text but Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.5C in Tables 1 and 2 (0.8 vs 0.5 C); this entry follows the 0.8C designation.

DFT lattice parameters of κ-related compounds increase with Mn substitution, from 3.78 Å for Fe3AlC (Fe2MnAlC) to 3.84 Å for Mn3AlC; the calculated FeAl-B2 lattice parameter was slightly below the experimental value but in overall good agreement, and the Fe3AlC (L1′2) lattice constant is larger than that of Fe3Al-L12 because the octahedral C atom expands the cell.

DFT alternative elastic parameters (first method): FeAl (B0 164 GPa, Cα 0.54, G 81.5 GPa, E100 210 GPa, E111 333 GPa), Fe3Al (153, 0.12, 21, 60, 322), Fe3AlC(sp) (216, 2.39, 175, 477, 217), Mn3AlC (B0 −214, Cα −1.59, G −175, E100 −412, E111 −285); Fe3AlC shows the largest bulk modulus, shear modulus and E100 and the strongest anisotropy, while FeAl has the largest E111.

DFT density of states of the four κ-carbides (Fe3AlC, Fe2MnAlC, FeMn2AlC, Mn3AlC) have nearly identical shapes, differing essentially only by a rigid band shift due to Mn having one fewer electron than Fe; the ferromagnetic ground state of Fe3AlC is favoured by 30 meV/at with a magnetic moment of 1.1 μB/at.Fe, less than half that of Fe3Al, attributed to Fe-C interactions rather than to the lattice-parameter change.

Phonon (vibrational) band structures: FeAl and Fe3AlC both show an optical gap separating high-frequency branches from light Al atoms from low-frequency branches from heavy Fe atoms (gap ≈0.7 THz for FeAl; a sparse 20–26 THz group for Fe3AlC), whereas Fe3Al shows a continuous, gapless and dynamically stable spectrum — in contrast to literature reports of L12 instability within GGA, implying strong sensitivity to the choice of functional.

Methodological caveat stated by the authors: nano-indentation as performed cannot measure isolated nano-sized precipitates, only the compound hardness of particles within their surrounding matrix; varying indenter size or load would introduce an indentation size effect that could obscure the real influence of precipitate size and shape.
